After cloud computing comes space computing, obviously, right? There’s a neat irony here: Real-world clouds can interfere with optical satellite links. Cloud cover (along with atmospheric turbulence) can block the laser-based connections between satellites and ground stations, limiting how much data can be brought down to the data center and cloud services waiting for it. In other words, cloud services on the ground can be held back by the weather they are named after.

Networking conglomerate NTT wants to enable a new era of communications above the clouds (literally) with a combined set of space computing and lunar infrastructure developments that draw heavily on its work in photonics and light-based computing.

The organization’s optical space communication infrastructure is now being aligned with technologies supporting observation and space datacenter creation. The company is also working on lunar surface communication and lunar energy transmission.

Our 88 constellations just got one louder

Today, the International Astronomical Union recognizes 88 constellations in the sky; the NTT C89 project was launched in 2024 to unify and scale the company’s space-related projects and create what it believes could be the 89th constellation.

Speaking to an auditorium of about 200 Japanese press and one reporter from The New Stack during his company’s annual NTT R&D Forum, NTT president and CEO Akira Shimada said that optical ground stations can be blocked by clouds or struggle to receive signals because of atmospheric turbulence.

For Shimada and team, this is why our planet’s communications infrastructure needs to reach for the stars.

“As high-resolution observation data grows, the capacity that can be sent from satellite to ground by radio becomes a challenge.”

“As high-resolution observation data grows, the capacity that can be sent from satellite to ground by radio becomes a challenge,” said Shimada. “A low Earth orbit satellite can communicate directly with a ground receiving facility only during the limited time it passes overhead. In addition to technology that compensates for turbulence, a mechanism will be developed to select which ground station and communication path to connect to according to weather, satellite position and communication conditions.”

Satellite communications crosses the (cloud) chasm

He explained that NTT is developing optical links that connect satellites to one another and to the ground, relaying data from observation satellites to other satellites. Rather than waiting for a satellite to pass over an Earth-based receiving facility, information is delivered via a satellite that can connect to the ground at that exact moment, reducing wait time.

“As connected devices and data, including video, continue to grow and increase, satellite communications need greater capacity and higher quality,” said Shimada. “This field is of growing importance because satellite communications connect places that terrestrial networks struggle to reach, such as mountainous areas, the sea and remote islands”

He further stated that satellite communications at this level also serve as a means of communication when ground facilities are unusable in a disaster. So while image resolution continues to improve, disasters and wildfires now demand real-time delivery, in time for decisions on evacuation, firefighting and recovery. Hence the need to connect more fluidly in space.

Who knew about the lunar power shadow problem?

Not content to work on communications on Earth and in the ether above our planet’s atmosphere, NTT is also looking to enable lunar surface communication and lunar energy transmission. But lunar power isn’t simple; you know about the permanent lunar shadow challenge, right?

As we look to build lunar bases and perhaps one day lunar data centers, these facilities will obviously need solar energy to power them one day. But the Moon’s craters — many of which hold water ice deposits, which will also be essential — often haven’t seen sunlight for billions of years. Lunar scientists call these permanently shadowed regions (PSRs), and they exist because the Moon’s 1.5-degree axial tilt restricts sunlight from moving across the poles, leaving deep crater floors in permanent shadow.

NTT’s work fully recognizes this challenge and also extends to power transmission operations on the lunar surface itself.

“The moon’s craters — many of which hold water ice deposits, which will also be essential [in the construction of lunar datacenters] — often haven’t seen sunlight for billions of years. It’s what lunar scientists call lunar permanently shadowed regions (PSRs).”

“With expanded lunar activity in view, NTT research now covers optical communications to connect the Earth and the Moon in a stable manner; it also extends to work to enable power supply on the lunar surface. For wireless power transmission by laser, the challenges are suppressing the spread of the light and the efficiency of conversion to electricity,” clarified Shimada.

AI processing in space

He says that the “ultimate goal” is to link inter-satellite optical communications, AI processing in space, and terrestrial data centers and optical networks, supporting the understanding of disaster conditions, monitoring of the global environment, and communications in areas where connectivity is difficult.

In June, NTT and Ireland-based MBRYONICS signed a memorandum of understanding to research and develop space optical communications technologies, a step toward launching IOWN (the Innovative Optical and Wireless Network initiative) in space. In September, NTT signed an MoU to connect France-based Cailabs ‘ optical ground stations to NTT datacenters via NTT’s All-Photonics Network (APN), a pillar of the IOWN initiative.

“NTT is also working on concepts to place optical ground stations near datacentres, so that information arriving from space can be processed with low latency and delivered where it is needed.”

NTT future concepts work

NTT is also working on concepts to place optical ground stations near datacentres, so that information arriving from space can be processed with low latency and delivered where it is needed. By using datacentres and communication networks around the world, space and the ground will be connected in what the company promises is a seamless manner.

Figures to think about in this arena are the fact that low Earth orbit satellites move at approximately 8 km per second, that it is approximately 380,000 kilometers between the Earth and the Moon, and that some 230 petabytes per day is forecast to be the volume of satellite-to-ground data traffic by 2033, according to NTT.

The next crewed Artemis mission, Artemis III, is a low-Earth-orbit docking test. The first landing is penciled in for Artemis IV in 2028. Let’s hope Artemis III gets close enough to scout a nice crater for the first lunar data center.
